posts.hook: The 3 businesses at the top of Google get most of the calls. Here's how those 3 get picked.
posts.caption:
When a homeowner types "plumber near me," Google shows a little map with 3 businesses pinned on it. That's the Map Pack.

Those 3 spots get the bulk of the calls. Everyone below them is fighting over scraps.

Google picks the 3 on three things:

1. Relevance. Does your profile actually say you do the thing they searched?
2. Distance. How close are you to the person searching?
3. Prominence. Reviews, mentions, how known you are.

You can't move your shop. But relevance and prominence are 100% in your control.

Which of the 3 do you think you're weakest on? Tell me below.

posts.hook: Your Google Business Profile primary category might be quietly costing you jobs.
posts.caption:
Quick one you can fix in 2 minutes today.

Open your Google Business Profile and look at your primary category.

If you're an HVAC company and it says "Air conditioning contractor" but most of your money is furnace and heating work in winter, you're telling Google to show you for the wrong searches half the year.

Your primary category is the single biggest lever for what searches you show up in.

Pick the one that matches the work you actually want more of. Add the rest as secondary categories.

Go check yours right now. What's it set to?

Deep navy background, bold headline area 'CHECK YOUR PRIMARY CATEGORY'. Modern, minimal, 1:1, no real brand logos.

posts.hook: Reviews aren't just social proof. They're a ranking factor. Here's the part nobody tells you.
posts.caption:
Everyone says "get more reviews." True, but incomplete.

Google reads the words inside your reviews, not just the star count.

So a review that says "great service" helps less than one that says "fast water heater replacement in Tampa, showed up same day."

That second one tells Google what you do and where you do it, in a real customer's words.

You can't write fake reviews. But you can ask the right way:

"If you have a sec, would you mention what we fixed and the town you're in? Helps other folks nearby find us."

That one line in your ask changes everything.

posts.hook: Add your service area towns to your profile. Most contractors skip this and lose the next town over.
posts.caption:
If you're a service-area business (you go to the customer, you don't have walk-ins), your Google profile lets you list the towns you serve.

Most guys list one and move on.

List every town you actually drive to. Each one is a signal to Google that you're relevant for searches in that area.

Don't fake it. If you don't work a town, leave it off. But the towns you do cover and forgot to add? That's free relevance you're leaving on the table.

Go add your real service areas this week. Took me 5 minutes the first time.

posts.hook: This is what a local ranking climb actually looks like. Not overnight. Real.
posts.caption:
People expect local SEO to be a switch. It's not. It's a climb.

Here's the shape of a real one. Swap in your own numbers if you're tracking them:

Week 1 to 4: fix the profile, categories, service areas. Nothing visible yet.
Week 4 to 8: reviews start landing with the right words. You creep onto page 1.
Week 8 to 12: you break into the map pack for your easier search terms.
Month 4+: the bigger, harder terms start moving.

The contractors who win are the ones who didn't quit at week 3 because "nothing happened."

Something was happening. It just hadn't surfaced yet.

Where are you in this timeline right now?

posts.hook: NAP consistency sounds boring. It's one of the fastest ways to wreck your local rankings.
posts.caption:
NAP means Name, Address, Phone.

Google checks if those three match everywhere your business shows up. Your site, Yelp, Angi, the BBB, HomeAdvisor, old directory listings you forgot about.

If one says "Suite 200" and another says "Ste 200," if an old listing has your disconnected number from 2019, Google gets confused about which info is real.

Confused Google ranks you lower. It plays it safe.

Pick one exact version of your name, address, and phone. Make every listing match it letter for letter.

Boring? Yes. Works? Also yes.

Deep navy background, headline 'MAKE IT MATCH EVERYWHERE'. Minimal, 1:1, no real directory logos.

posts.hook: Post on your Google Business Profile like it's a free billboard. Because it is.
posts.caption:
Your Google Business Profile has a posts section most contractors never touch.

It's free space that shows up right on your listing when someone's deciding whether to call you.

You don't need to be a writer. Post:

A before/after photo from a recent job.
A "we have same-day openings this week" note.
A quick tip your customers always ask about.

Keep it to a sentence or two. Post weekly.

It signals to Google you're active and gives the person reading a reason to pick you over the dead-looking profile next to yours.

What job photo could you post today?

posts.hook: "Near me" searches don't include a town name. Here's how Google decides who's near.
posts.caption:
When someone searches "electrician near me," they don't type a town. So how does Google know who to show?

It uses the searcher's phone location, right then, in real time.

That means your ranking literally changes depending on where the person is standing. You might be #1 from the customer's driveway and #6 from across town.

Two takeaways:

1. Being physically central to your service area is an advantage you can't buy.
2. Since you can't move, you win the edges with relevance and reviews so Google stretches your reach further out.

This is why one fixed rank report is misleading. Local is a map, not a number.

posts.hook: Add real photos to your profile every month. Google notices, and so do customers.
posts.caption:
Stock photos do nothing for you. Real ones do a lot.

Google Business Profiles with regular, real photos get more clicks and more direction requests. Google reads activity as a sign you're a legit, running business.

You're already on jobs all day. Snap two photos per job:

The problem you walked into.
The finished work.

Upload a batch every month. Geotagged from the job site is a bonus.

This costs you nothing but 10 seconds on site. Set a reminder for the first of the month and just do it.

posts.hook: There are two Googles fighting over your customer: the map and the blue links. You need both.
posts.caption:
When someone searches for a home service, the results page has two zones:

The Map Pack up top. Three local businesses with pins, reviews, a call button.

The organic links below it. Regular web pages that rank for the search.

Most contractors obsess over the map and ignore the links. Mistake.

The map gets you the "call right now" customer. The organic pages catch the "researching, comparing, reading" customer who buys next week.

Your Google Business Profile feeds the map. Your website content feeds the organic links. Strong businesses show up in both, so they catch the customer no matter how they search.

Which zone are you currently winning?

posts.hook: Answer the Q&A on your own profile before a competitor or a troll does it for you.
posts.caption:
Your Google Business Profile has a questions section. Anyone can post a question. And anyone can answer it. Including people who don't work for you.

That's a problem if you ignore it.

Do this: post the questions your customers always ask, and answer them yourself.

"Do you offer emergency service?"
"Do you charge for estimates?"
"What areas do you cover?"

Now the right answers are locked in, in your words, before someone else fills the gap with a wrong one.

Bonus: those answers often contain the exact phrases people search, which helps relevance.

Go seed 3 questions on your profile today.

posts.hook: The cheapest lead you'll ever get is the one already searching for you. Local SEO is how you catch it.
posts.caption:
Think about where a job actually comes from.

Paid ads: you pay per click, every click, forever. Stop paying, leads stop.

Referrals: great, but you can't control the volume.

Local search: someone with a broken AC types "ac repair near me" and Google hands them three options. If you're one of the three, that lead cost you nothing per click.

That's the whole pitch for local SEO. It's not magic. It's putting your business in front of people at the exact second they need you, without paying a toll on every single click.

The work is upfront. The leads compound after.

How are most of your jobs coming in right now?

posts.hook: Schema markup is just a label that tells Google what your page is. Here's why it matters to a plumber.
posts.caption:
Schema markup sounds like developer stuff. The idea is simple.

It's hidden code on your website that labels things for Google in a language Google trusts. "This is a business. This is the phone. These are the hours. This is the service area. These are the reviews."

Without it, Google has to guess by reading your page like a person. With it, you hand Google the facts directly.

That's how you get those rich results: the star ratings, the FAQ dropdowns, the business info box that shows up before anyone clicks.

You don't have to write it by hand. The point is to know it exists and make sure your site has it. Most home service sites don't.

Does yours? If you're not sure, that's worth checking.

Deep navy background, headline 'LABEL IT FOR GOOGLE'. Clean dev-themed vector, 1:1.

Here's a move most people don't think to make.

The free audit works on any website, not just yours.

So run it on the competitor who keeps beating you to the top of the map.

You'll see their profile setup, their content depth, their review situation, their directory presence. The gap between you and them stops being a mystery and becomes a checklist.

Then run it on yourself and compare side by side.

Knowing exactly why they outrank you is worth more than any guess. Link in bio. Go scout the competition.

posts.hook: One service, one page. Stop cramming everything onto your homepage.
posts.caption:
Common mistake on home service sites: the homepage lists all 12 services in a paragraph and that's it.

Google can't rank one page for 12 different searches well. It ranks pages that go deep on one thing.

So if you do drain cleaning, water heaters, and repiping, that's three pages, not three lines on one page.

Each page should actually talk about that service. The common problems, what the job involves, roughly what to expect. Written for the customer, not stuffed with keywords.

More real pages, each focused, means more searches you can rank for. It adds up fast.

How many of your services have their own real page right now?

posts.hook: Google now answers questions with AI. Your business can get cited there too. Here's the basics.
posts.caption:
You've seen it. You search something and Google writes an answer at the top, pulling from different sites.

That's the AI overview. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity do the same thing.

More people are getting answers there without clicking any website at all. That's a shift you can't ignore.

The good news: these AI answers cite sources. Businesses with clear, well-structured content that directly answers real questions get pulled in.

So the same things that win local search, clear service pages, real answers to real questions, plain language, also get you mentioned by the AI.

Write for a human asking a real question and you're already most of the way there.

Have you searched your own service lately to see what the AI says?

posts.hook: Two plumbers, same town, same skills. One gets the calls. The only difference is who shows up on Google.
posts.caption:
Picture two plumbers in the same town. Same license, same quality work, same prices.

Plumber A has a clean Google profile, the right categories, 80 reviews that mention real jobs, a website with a page per service.

Plumber B does great work and has a profile he set up once in 2021 and never touched.

A homeowner's pipe bursts at 7pm. They grab their phone. "Emergency plumber near me."

They will never see Plumber B. Not because B is worse. Because B is invisible at the exact moment that customer is ready to call.

The job goes to whoever shows up. Local SEO is just making sure that's you.

Which plumber's profile is closer to yours right now?

posts.hook: Reply to every review, even the one-liners. It's a ranking signal and a trust signal at once.
posts.caption:
Replying to reviews does two jobs at the same time.

One, Google sees an active, engaged business and that helps your prominence.

Two, the next customer reading sees how you handle people, good and bad.

For a good review: thank them, and naturally mention the service and town. "Thanks Mike, glad we got the AC back up fast for you in Brandon." Now that reply has keywords too.

For a bad review: stay calm, professional, brief. The reply isn't for the angry person. It's for the 50 people who read it later and judge how you carry yourself.

Never argue. Never get personal. Reply to all of them.

What's your current reply rate, honestly?

posts.hook: Citations are just other websites listing your business. Quality beats quantity, and here's the order.
posts.caption:
A citation is any other site that lists your business name, address, and phone. Yelp, Angi, the chamber of commerce, your trade association, local directories.

They matter because each consistent listing is another vote that your business is real and located where you say.

But not all citations are equal. The order that actually matters:

1. The big ones first. Google, Yelp, Facebook, Apple Maps, the major industry directories for your trade.
2. Local ones next. Your chamber, local news, local sponsorships.
3. Then the long tail of general directories.

Don't blast your info into 500 junk directories. Get the important ones right and consistent. That's where the weight is.

Which of the big ones are you missing?

posts.hook: Put your phone number in text on your site, not buried in an image. Sounds dumb. Costs people calls.
posts.caption:
Real one I see all the time.

A contractor puts their phone number inside a logo image or a banner graphic. Looks fine on desktop.

Then a customer pulls up the site on their phone, ready to call, and they can't tap the number because it's a picture, not text.

They bounce. You never knew they were there.

Fix: your phone number should be real text, near the top, and on mobile it should be a tap-to-call link. Same for your address linking to maps.

Make it stupid easy to contact you. The easiest competitor to reach often wins, even over the better one.

Go pull up your own site on your phone right now and try to call yourself.

posts.hook: Google judges your site speed on mobile now. Slow site, lower rank, lost calls. The fix is usually simple.
posts.caption:
Most of your customers find you on a phone, often on cell data, often in a hurry because something broke.

Google knows this, so it factors how fast your site loads on mobile into your ranking. Slow site, you slide down.

Worse than the ranking hit: people just leave. A few seconds of staring at a blank screen and they're back to the search results calling the next guy.

The usual culprit is huge images. A 5MB photo of a finished roof loads like molasses on data.

The fix is rarely a full rebuild. It's usually compressing images and cutting the junk plugins. Cheap wins.

When did you last load your own site on cell data, not wifi?

posts.hook: The work you do in June is the rankings you get in September. Local SEO pays the patient.
posts.caption:
Here's the part that trips people up.

Local SEO has a delay between the work and the result. You fix things now, Google reacts over weeks, the rankings move later.

That delay is exactly why most contractors quit and most never start. No instant scoreboard, so it feels like nothing's working.

Flip it. The delay is also the moat. The guy who started six months ago is sitting in the map pack right now while you're deciding whether to begin.

If you'd planted the work six months ago, you'd be ranking today. The next best time is this week.

The contractors who own their local market aren't smarter. They just started earlier and didn't stop.

What would six months of steady work put you in position for?

posts.hook: Match your website words to how customers actually talk, not industry terms.
posts.caption:
You might call it "HVAC system diagnostics." Your customer calls it "my ac isn't blowing cold."

Google matches searches to pages. If your site only uses the industry term and the customer searches the plain one, you can miss the match.

Write your pages in customer words. The symptoms they describe. The way they'd say it to a friend.

"Furnace won't turn on."
"Water heater leaking."
"Breaker keeps tripping."

Those phrases are exactly what people type. Put them on your pages, in headings and in plain sentences, because that's the bridge between their problem and your phone number.

Write for the panicked homeowner, not the trade journal.

What's the most common way customers describe what you fix?

posts.hook: Holiday weekend? Set your Google hours now so you don't show 'open' when you're closed.
posts.caption:
Quick one for the long weekend.

If your Google Business Profile says you're open today and someone calls and gets voicemail, that's a bad experience Google notices and a customer you annoyed.

Google lets you set special holiday hours. Use them.

Closed for the 4th? Set it. Running an emergency-only schedule? Note it in a profile post so people know how to reach you for true emergencies.

Nothing tanks trust faster than "open" hours that aren't real. Two minutes now saves a frustrated would-be customer later.

Go set your holiday hours before you fire up the grill. Have a good 4th.

posts.hook: Backlinks for a local business aren't about thousands of links. It's about a handful of local ones.
posts.caption:
Backlinks are other sites linking to yours. For big national brands, it's an arms race for thousands.

For a local home service business, you're playing a different, easier game.

A few quality local links do real work:

Your local chamber of commerce.
A supplier or manufacturer's "find a pro" page.
The little league team or charity you sponsor.
Local news if you do something newsworthy.
Your trade association directory.

Each one says "this business is real and rooted in this community." That's exactly the signal Google wants for local.

You don't need a marketing degree. You need to show up in your own town's web presence.

Who in your community could link to you that already knows your name?

Start at the top of that list. Knock out one thing a week. In a few months you won't recognize your local rankings.

Or have us run the whole cycle for you. Either way, the audit is the place to start. Link in bio.

Save this post so the list is there when you're ready.

posts.hook: The whole game in one sentence: be the most obvious choice when your neighbor needs you.
posts.caption:
Strip away all the tactics and local SEO comes down to one thing.

When someone near you needs what you do, you want to be the obvious, easy, trustworthy choice staring back at them on that screen.

Every piece we've talked about serves that one goal:

Right categories so you show up for the right search.
Reviews so you look trustworthy at a glance.
Fast, clear site so calling you is effortless.
Real content so Google and the customer both understand what you do.

It's not tricks. It's being genuinely, clearly the best answer to a local search, and making that answer easy for Google to read.

Do that and the calls follow. That's the whole thing.

Follow along, more next month. And if you want it handled for you, the link's always in the bio.
